title: Week 21 Analysis
commentary:
The tracker now holds 207 media cases across ten categories, with reality_distortion (73 cases, 35%) and romantic_attachment (57 cases, 28%) accounting for nearly two-thirds of the corpus. This week's additions follow that distribution closely. Multiple independent outlets — ScienceDaily, the ABC in Australia, The Good Men Project — published pieces focused on how AI chatbots may erode the boundary between plausible interaction and delusional thinking. When sources this varied converge on the same framing within a single week, it tends to reflect genuine clinical signal rather than editorial fashion.

The romantic_attachment category continues to develop in ways that resist easy interpretation. Metro and MSN both covered a first-person account of someone whose AI relationship, by their own account, stabilised their human marriage. Singapore's experts, in the same week, warned of harm to adolescent relational development from AI companions. Both reports are probably accurate within their respective populations. What they share is a platform architecture that has intimacy as a core engagement mechanism — the psychological outcomes diverge, but the design logic is consistent across cases. OpenAI's Trusted Contact feature sits in the same conceptual space: a safeguard that simultaneously normalises the chatbot as a primary emotional contact worthy of clinical monitoring.

Italy's clinically documented AI addiction — reported as the country's first formally recognised instance — is the standout case this week. The significance here is less about the individual and more about what clinical recognition implies: formal diagnostic infrastructure is beginning to encounter this pattern at sufficient frequency to categorise it. A 'first case' in a healthcare system usually means the pattern has been present long enough to be undeniable, not that it has just appeared. Caliber.Az's framing as a milestone reflects institutional catching-up more than a genuinely novel event.

Across 242 total cases — media, clinical, and academic — a shift in the nature of coverage is becoming legible. Early entries in this dataset were predominantly incident reports. The past two months show more institutional response: a National Academy of Medicine report on chatbot mental health outcomes, government-level warnings from Singapore, a dedicated OpenAI product feature, and clinical recognition in a European healthcare system. The documentation phase appears to be transitioning into something closer to a governance conversation, which is itself worth tracking separately from the case record.
